artifact.title: Detection & analysis
objectives: Explain detection & analysis using a scoped evidence-to-decision model
Apply a safe, repeatable detection & analysis workflow to a workplace simulation
Evaluate evidence and verify a defensive outcome related to detection & analysis

blocks.text: Detection & analysis is taught here as an operational capability inside Incident Response Foundations, not as an isolated definition. Incident response is a coordinated risk-management process. Teams prepare, detect, analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, communicate, and learn while preserving the evidence needed for sound decisions. In this module, your job is to build a reliable mental model. Start by naming the system or decision in scope, the assumptions you are making, and the outcome that would count as success. Then connect detection & analysis to observable evidence and an accountable decision owner. This structure prevents vocabulary from becoming false confidence and makes later lab and project work reproducible.

Use a five-part workflow. First, define the authorized scope and the question you are trying to answer. Second, preserve a baseline so later changes can be explained or reversed. Third, collect the smallest sufficient evidence; for this course that commonly includes incident scope, affected identities and assets, timeline, containment state, eradication checks, and recovery telemetry. Fourth, compare at least two plausible explanations and select a proportionate action. Fifth, verify the resulting state with a different observation where practical, record limitations, and identify who owns follow-up. The same workflow applies whether detection & analysis is used for prevention, investigation, engineering, or communication.

blocks.heading: Evidence standard
blocks.body: Evidence quality matters more than volume. Prefer records that identify source, time, affected entity, collection method, and relevant configuration or context. Separate direct observations from inferences, and do not silently discard contradictory data. A strong note explains why an artifact supports the conclusion, how it could be misleading, and what additional check would change confidence. For detection & analysis, capture enough context that another learner can reproduce the reasoning without receiving a hidden answer or relying on the original operator’s memory.

blocks.heading: From weak activity to professional evidence
rows: State scope and gather traceable evidence
Compare the resulting state with success criteria

blocks.body: Consider this approved workplace simulation: an organization investigates a suspected account compromise while critical business work continues. The team must reason about detection & analysis. A careful analyst records the starting condition, identifies the relevant decision and evidence owners, gathers incident scope, affected identities and assets, timeline, containment state, eradication checks, and recovery telemetry, and compares the observation with the expected state. The analyst applies one bounded change or recommendation, checks both the intended outcome and likely side effects, and records residual uncertainty. The final report describes what was observed, what was inferred, what was changed, how recovery or cleanup was verified, and what should be monitored next.

A common failure is taking a disruptive containment action before understanding scope, dependencies, evidence needs, and business impact. That approach feels fast but breaks traceability and can increase impact. Instead, pause when scope, evidence origin, authorization, or the success criterion is unclear. Ask what an independent reviewer would need to reproduce the decision. Tool output, model output, alert names, and copied commands are inputs—not authority. The learner remains responsible for validating the result and staying inside the approved environment.

blocks.heading: Defense, authorization, and cleanup
blocks.body: Defensive practice must accompany every concept: use rehearsed playbooks, decision authority, evidence preservation, bounded containment, recovery monitoring, and lessons learned. For dual-use subjects, all activity stays inside the supplied local simulation; never transfer targets, credentials, payloads, or techniques to public systems. Good work includes remediation and retesting, not merely identifying a weakness. It also protects sensitive evidence and explains uncertainty in language appropriate for technical and nontechnical stakeholders.

Before continuing, write one direct observation, one hypothesis, one bounded action, and one independent verification step for detection & analysis. If authorization or evidence is missing, the correct decision is to stop and obtain it.

Detection & analysis becomes job-ready evidence when the learner can define scope, preserve and interpret relevant observations, choose a proportionate action, verify the outcome, and communicate limitations. The quiz checks this reasoning; the course lab and project require the same chain in a larger scenario.

check.question: How should a learner verify that a control related to Detection & analysis worked?
options: Assume success when the configuration command returns no error.
Define the expected state, test it with independent evidence, and record residual risk or follow-up work.
Measure only whether the control was purchased or enabled.
Skip retesting when the original issue is no longer visible to one tool.
